noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: understand that a balanced diet should include appropriate proportions of carbohydrate, protein, lipid, vitamins, minerals, water and dietary fibre

identify the sources and describe the functions of carbohydrate, protein, lipid (fats and oils), vitamins A, C and D, the mineral ions calcium and iron, water and dietary fibre as components of the diet
understand how energy requirements vary with activity levels, age and pregnancy

primer.text: You know food fuels the body and that different meals feel different. This lesson formalises that: what a balanced diet actually contains, what each dietary element does and where it comes from, how malnutrition damages health, and why a growing child, an athlete and an expectant mother all need different quantities.

lessons.title: Balance, Malnutrition and Its Costs
sourceHeadings: The Importance of a Balanced Diet
Causes and effects of malnutrition table
lessons.opening: A balanced diet serves every food group in the right proportion: carbohydrate, protein, lipid, dietary fibre, vitamins, mineral ions and water. Skew those proportions and malnutrition follows, bringing a recognisable set of health problems that the corpus table lays out cause by cause.
keyPoints: A balanced diet means all food groups present in correct proportions.
An unbalanced diet leads to malnutrition.
Malnutrition produces a range of human health problems.
The seven key groups are carbohydrate, protein, lipid, fibre, vitamins, minerals and water.
The malnutrition table pairs each dietary cause with its effect.

low.restatement: Right amounts of everything: that is balance; wrong amounts bring malnutrition.
low.analogy: An orchestra needs every section at the right volume — one blaring section ruins the piece.
low.examPointer: List all seven groups by name; naming six loses the mark.

medium.restatement: Balance is about proportion, not abundance — even healthful groups distort the diet in excess.
medium.analogy: A recipe ruined by too much of one good ingredient.
medium.examPointer: Expect a table-completion question pairing causes of malnutrition with effects.

check.stem: Which set lists the key groups of a balanced diet?

options.text: Carbohydrate, protein, lipid, dietary fibre, vitamins, minerals and water
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Three groups cannot cover the diet.
Salt is not one of the seven named groups.
Sugar is not a separate key group here.

options.text: The health problems caused by an unbalanced diet
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: Eating too much of every group
options.explanation: Malnutrition covers both excess and shortage.
Water shortage is one cause among many.
Malnutrition is dietary, not genetic.

check.stem: Why does proportion matter more than abundance in a balanced diet?

options.text: Each group has a job, and excess of one cannot replace another group's function
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Cost is not the biological issue.

options.text: Because all groups taste better mixed
options.explanation: Taste is irrelevant to the definition.

options.text: Because the body stores every group equally
options.explanation: Groups are handled quite differently by the body.

check.stem: Which statement about the malnutrition table is correct?

options.text: It pairs dietary causes with the health effects they produce
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: It ranks foods by energy content
options.explanation: Energy ranking is a different table.
The table covers malnutrition generally.
Quantities belong to the requirements topic.

check.stem: A diet lacking dietary fibre mainly affects which system?

options.text: The intestine, which needs the bulk to move food along
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
That is vitamin A's role.
That is calcium and vitamin D.
That is iron's role.

check.modelAnswer: A diet that includes all food groups in the correct proportions for health.

check.stem: Name the condition caused by an unbalanced diet.
check.modelAnswer: That condition is malnutrition, which brings a variety of health problems.

check.stem: Explain why no single food group can sustain health alone.
check.modelAnswer: Because each group performs a different job — energy, growth, insulation, bulk, regulation and reaction medium — and none of them covers another's function, so leaving a group out starves the body of that job no matter how much of the others is eaten.

check.stem: A friend eats only protein shakes and rice. Use the balanced-diet idea to advise them.
check.modelAnswer: Their diet omits lipid, vitamins, minerals, fibre and most water sources, so it is unbalanced and risks malnutrition; they should add vegetables, fruits, oils and dairy or fish to restore all seven groups in proportion.

lessons.title: Dietary Elements and Energy Needs
lessons.opening: Each dietary element has a defined function and source: carbohydrate for energy from bread and rice, protein for growth and repair from meat and pulses, lipid for insulation and storage, fibre for bulk, vitamins and minerals for health maintenance, and water for chemical reactions. Requirements then shift with age, activity and pregnancy.
keyPoints: Carbohydrate supplies energy from sources like bread, cereals, pasta and rice.
Protein drives growth and repair; meat, fish, eggs and pulses supply it.
Lipid insulates and stores energy; butter, oil and nuts provide it.
Calcium builds bones and teeth; vitamin D helps absorb calcium; iron feeds haemoglobin.
Children need more protein proportionally, and active people need more energy overall.
Pregnancy raises energy needs and adds calcium and iron for the developing fetus.

low.restatement: Every element has a function, a source list, and a deficiency disease.
low.analogy: A toolbox: each tool has a job and a place it lives.
low.examPointer: Learn element-function-source-deficiency as four linked facts per nutrient.

medium.restatement: Deficiency diseases name the failure: scurvy without vitamin C, rickets without vitamin D, anaemia without iron.
medium.analogy: A factory line stopping when one part runs out.
medium.examPointer: Pair each vitamin or mineral with its exact deficiency condition by name.

check.stem: Which nutrient's function is insulation and energy storage?

options.text: Lipid, from sources such as butter, oil and nuts
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Carbohydrate is the quick energy source.
Protein builds and repairs.
Fibre provides intestinal bulk.

check.stem: Which mineral ion helps blood to clot and strengthens teeth and bones?

options.text: Calcium, found in milk, cheese and eggs
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Iron builds haemoglobin for oxygen transport.
Vitamin C is a vitamin, not a mineral ion, and serves collagen.
Vitamin A serves the retina's pigment.

check.stem: Which vitamin or mineral shortage pairs with its condition correctly?

options.text: Vitamin D shortage leading to rickets in children
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Scurvy follows vitamin C shortage.

options.text: Vitamin C shortage leading to osteoporosis
options.explanation: Osteoporosis links to long-term calcium shortage.
Anaemia follows iron shortage.

check.stem: Why do children need a higher proportion of protein than adults?

options.text: Protein is required for growth, which is rapid in childhood
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Protein is not stored for insulation.
Adults digest protein normally.
Blood loss is not the daily driver of protein need.

check.stem: Why does pregnancy raise energy requirements?

options.text: The developing fetus needs energy to grow, and the mother carries extra mass
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: The mother breathes faster at rest
options.explanation: Breathing rate is not the stated cause.

options.text: The fetus filters the mother's blood
options.explanation: The placenta handles exchange, not the fetus directly.
Breastfeeding comes after birth.

check.stem: State the function of dietary fibre.
check.modelAnswer: Fibre provides the bulk that helps the intestine push food through.

check.stem: Name the pigment that iron helps to build.
check.modelAnswer: Iron builds the haemoglobin pigment that red blood cells use to carry oxygen.

check.stem: Explain why vitamin D and calcium are often discussed together.
check.modelAnswer: Because vitamin D enables the body to absorb calcium, so even a calcium-rich diet fails when vitamin D is lacking; both are needed for strong bones and teeth, and shortages of either can damage bone health.

check.stem: A breastfeeding mother plans her meals. Which adjustments does the corpus guidance imply?
check.modelAnswer: She should raise her energy intake, since breastfeeding demands extra energy, and keep calcium levels up because calcium feeds the production of rich breast milk.

glossary.definition: A diet supplying every food group in the correct proportions.
The health problems that follow an unbalanced diet.
The iron-based pigment in red blood cells that carries oxygen.
The childhood bone-condition caused by severe vitamin D shortage.
